sounds.intro: Norwegian (Bokmål) is written in the Latin alphabet with three extra letters at the end: æ, ø, å. Nouns are "en", "ei" or "et" words. The language has a sing-song pitch, and long and short vowels matter.
rows: like "a" in "cat", but longer before r
say "ur" with rounded lips, like "ur" in "fur"
say "ee" with rounded lips, like German "ü"
a rounded "ew", like a short "oo" said with the lips forward
often sounds like "sh" in the east of Norway
g / k before i, y, ei, ø
k and g become soft, like "ch" and "y"
notes: Double consonants make the vowel before them short. A single consonant after a stressed vowel means the vowel is long.
Norwegian is spoken with two pitch patterns. Listen and copy the melody of whole words.

grammar.title: Pronouns
text: Norwegian always uses the pronoun. "Du" is you. "Han" is he, "hun" is she, "det" or "den" is it. The polite "De" is old-fashioned.

grammar.title: Singular and plural
text: Nouns are "en", "ei" or "et" words. Plurals end in -er, -e, or have no ending. Learn the plural with each noun.

grammar.title: To be: være
text: "Å være" (to be) has one form for everyone in the present: er.

grammar.title: Ha: have
text: "Å ha" (to have) is "har" in the present for everyone. "Det er" or "det finnes" means "there is".

grammar.title: Present tense
text: Add -er to the stem. Å arbeide (to work): jeg arbeider. The ending is the same for every person.

grammar.title: Basic sentences
text: The verb is always the second item: Jeg leser en bok. If another word comes first, the verb still stays second: I dag leser jeg en bok.

grammar.title: Negation
text: Put "ikke" after the verb: Jeg går ikke. In questions and with a second verb, "ikke" comes after the subject.
ex: I do not have a car
he does not work on Sundays

grammar.title: Asking questions
text: Put the verb first: Er du elev? A question word goes before the verb: Hvor bor du?

grammar.title: Question words
text: A question word comes first, then the verb.

grammar.title: Possessives and liking
text: The word agrees with the noun: min / mi / mitt / mine (my), din / di / ditt / dine (your), hans, hennes, vår / vårt / våre (our), deres (their, your plural). To like something, use "å like".

grammar.title: Formal vs informal
text: Norwegian almost always uses "du", even with strangers and older people. "De" is old-fashioned and sounds stiff. Use "du".

grammar.title: Past and future (simple)
text: Past: add -et, -te, -de, or a changed stem. Jeg arbeidet (I worked), jeg gikk (I went). Future: "skal", "vil" or "kommer til å" + verb.

grammar.title: Commands
text: Use the bare stem: kom. Add "vær så snill" to be polite. To forbid, use "ikke".

grammar.title: Can, must, want
text: Kunne (can): jeg kan. Måtte (must): jeg må. Ville (want): jeg vil. The second verb stays in its basic form.
ex: I do not want to eat

grammar.title: In, on, at
text: Common words: i (in), på (on, at), ved (at, by), til (to), fra (from), med (with), under (under).
ex: the book is on the table
the cat is under the table
the shop is next to the bank
butikken ligger ved siden av banken
bew-TIK-ken LIG-ger veh SEE-den ah BAN-ken
the park is near the station
the key is in the bag

grammar.title: Comparing things
text: Add -ere for "more", -est for "the most": fin, finere, fineste. Some are irregular: stor, større, størst. "Than" is "enn".
